newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Competition to benefit NZ mortgage holders in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Competition to benefit NZ mortgage holders in 1997.

text.p: Borrowers are set to benefit in 1997 as banks and non-bank lenders provide stiff competition in the mortgage lending market, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Monday.
"The banks are certainly seeking to fight us for every mortgage that comes along," managing director of AMP -- parent to new non-bank Ergo Financial Services -- Rodney Cook told NZPA.

Ergo was the first among new nationwide non-bank lenders. Sovereign Financial Services and New Zealand Home Loans also set up shop this year. The three have been early movers in interest rate reductions through the year and their rates have been the lowest.

An NZPA source within one of the major traditional banks recognised the overheads advantage the new entrants had through not having to support nationwide branch networks, and their sometimes lower fees.

The majors are playing down the size of the threat. They point out the industry as a whole is restructuring away from expensive face-to-face branch transactions and they will compete through better service. Banks aim to split off daily transactions into cheaper electronic banking, leaving "service centres" to offer personal consultation on products like mortgages, superannuation and insurance.
Ergo managing director Graham Meyer estimated the non-bank share of the mortgage market to have reached 3-4 percent in 1996, with Ergo making up a substantial part of that.
The new non-bank lenders look to the Australian example and predict their share could rise to as much as 20 percent over the next year, putting further pressure on industry margins.

However, across the Tasman, ANZ Banking Group chief executive Don Mercer said the growth of non-banks there had come to an end and would stay at about 10 percent. They would have to manage costs and live with less growth to survive.
"There seems to be an ongoing place for specialist mortgage originators, but fundamentally anything they can do the banks can do at least as well," Mercer said.
Banking analysts expect this frustrated growth to spill over into New Zealand.

But professor of banking at Massey University, Chris Moore, questioned how long the new operators would be able to undercut New Zealand banks. In contrast, Australian banking margins had been reasonably "fat".
"The banks will meet them, in the end, or will be just above them. Will people shift for a quarter of a percentage point (off a mortgage) and possibly lose a higher level of service?"

Financial Services Federation executive director Justin Kerr said it was "extraordinarily ambitious'' to expect non-bank lenders to make the kind of inroads in New Zealand that their counterparts had made in Australia. Margins here were so much narrower.

Securitisation gave some non-banks a funding advantage over lenders trading through the wholesale money market, he said. But the new entrants were a long way from achieving the NZ$1 billion worth of loans local building societies held on their books.
Total residential home mortgages held industry-wide amount to $41 billion.

Whatever happens, interest rate margins will remain tight as competition in the current environment is compounded by new non-bank entrants and more large offshore banks arriving to focus solely on mortgages.
